questions.text: Which model and image-resolution tier should be the default for naming?
questions.context: This is the entire bill. RESEARCH.md puts a Retina screenshot at ~1560 visual tokens on the standard tier, so at Haiku 4.5's $1/M input the whole ~4000-file backlog is roughly $6. A larger model or the high-resolution tier multiplies that by several times; the high-resolution tier is also the only option that keeps small UI text legible in the pixels the model actually sees.

options.label: Haiku 4.5, standard resolution tier (default)
options.tradeoff: ~$6 for 4000 files, but 11px UI text is illegible after downscaling, so the name leans almost entirely on the OCR text in the prompt.

options.label: Haiku 4.5, high-resolution tier
options.tradeoff: ~3x the visual tokens (order of $20 for the backlog); the model can actually read the screenshot, which mostly matters for captures OCR handles badly.

options.label: Sonnet 5, standard resolution tier
options.tradeoff: Meaningfully better at judging what a screenshot is *about* rather than what it says; several times Haiku's per-image price, so a backlog run in the tens of dollars.

options.label: Start on Haiku and let --sample decide
options.tradeoff: Costs cents to compare tiers on 30 real files before committing, but adds a step before you can start the real run.

questions.text: Synchronous API with bounded concurrency, or the Batch API?
questions.context: The Batch API is 50% cheaper and has a far higher throughput ceiling, which suits a one-shot backlog; the synchronous path is low-latency, which is what the sample-and-iterate loop needs. Supporting both is real extra machinery (job submission, polling, result reconciliation) and changes the pipeline from streaming to two-phase.

options.label: Synchronous only, bounded concurrency (default)
options.tradeoff: Simplest pipeline, instant feedback while iterating on the prompt; pays full price and takes tens of minutes for the full backlog.

options.label: Batch API for the full run, synchronous for --sample
options.tradeoff: Halves the bill and removes rate-limit pressure entirely; adds job-lifecycle code and turns the main run into a kick-off-and-check-later job.

options.label: Batch API only
options.tradeoff: Cheapest and simplest to reason about at scale, but every prompt iteration on a 30-file sample now waits on a batch job.

questions.text: Should --apply be able to run without a saved plan, or must it execute a plan file?
questions.context: If --apply always consumes a plan.jsonl produced by an earlier dry run (AC-034), the names you approved are exactly the names you get, and apply becomes a pure filesystem operation with no model calls. If --apply can generate and rename in one pass, it is one command instead of two but nothing you reviewed is guaranteed to be what lands.

options.label: Both: --apply generates in one pass, --plan replays an approved plan (default)
options.tradeoff: Convenient and flexible; the one-pass path renames names no human ever saw, which at thousands of files is where a bad prompt tweak does its damage.

options.label: Strict two-phase: --apply requires --plan
options.tradeoff: Impossible to rename anything you did not review, and apply is fast and offline; every run is two commands even when you already trust the output.

questions.text: Should v1 include a corpus-level pass to fight generic-name collapse?
questions.context: Per-file naming has no knowledge of the corpus, so you get 'terminal-output' forty times and 'safari-browser-window' a hundred times - individually reasonable, collectively useless. The date prefix keeps them unique but not distinguishable. Fixing it properly means a second pass that detects low-entropy or repeated names and re-prompts with more context, which is more code, a second round of API calls for those files, and a non-streaming pipeline.

options.label: No corpus pass in v1; rely on the date prefix and hash suffixes (default)
options.tradeoff: Simple, cheap, streaming; the folder still contains dozens of near-identical names differing only by date.

options.label: Detect repeated slugs and re-prompt those files for specificity
options.tradeoff: Directly attacks the main quality complaint; costs a second model call for the repeat offenders (likely 10-25% of files) and requires holding the full name set before applying.

options.label: Full clustering pass over near-duplicate screenshots first
options.tradeoff: Best possible names and it also catches the burst-of-three-identical-captures case; substantially more work and the most expensive option to build and run.

questions.text: How aggressively should the tool abstain from naming?
questions.context: You chose to leave meaningless screenshots untouched rather than name them generically. The remaining knob is where the line sits. Abstaining too eagerly leaves a folder half-renamed; abstaining too rarely produces confident names for black screens.

options.label: Conservative: abstain only on clearly empty images - under 12 OCR characters AND low entropy (default)
options.tradeoff: Almost never abstains on something nameable; lets through cropped dialogs with six words that get thin, low-value names.

options.label: Aggressive: also abstain when the model's own confidence is low or the name is one generic segment
options.tradeoff: Every name that survives is worth having; likely leaves 25-35% of the folder with original names, so the folder stays visibly mixed.

questions.text: How should non-Latin text in a screenshot be handled in the filename?
questions.context: Apple Vision reads CJK, Cyrillic, and accented Latin fine, but the ASCII-slug rule (AC-017) throws that away. The 255-byte filesystem limit is byte-based, so a CJK name hits the wall at roughly 85 visible characters.

options.label: Transliterate to ASCII, drop what cannot be transliterated (default)
options.tradeoff: Every filename is safe in every tool and shell; a Japanese UI screenshot becomes a romanized or generic name you may not recognize.

options.label: Allow NFC-normalized Unicode in slugs, still stripping / and : and enforcing 255 bytes
options.tradeoff: Names stay faithful to what was on screen; reintroduces exactly the class of invisible-character and encoding bugs this tool exists to survive.

questions.text: Should --max-cost have a default ceiling, or be opt-in?
questions.context: A guard that aborts before the first request if the estimate exceeds a threshold. With no default, a mistyped path pointed at a 40,000-file folder bills you ten times what you expected before you notice.

options.label: No default ceiling; --max-cost is opt-in (default)
options.tradeoff: Never blocks a legitimate large run; nothing stands between a typo and a surprise bill.

options.label: Default ceiling of $15, overridable per run
options.tradeoff: A runaway run stops itself with a message stating the estimate; you will occasionally have to re-run with a raised ceiling for a genuinely big job.

questions.text: Which Apple OCR path should stage 1 use?
questions.context: RESEARCH.md notes that since Sonoma the newer Live Text path reportedly outperforms classic VisionKit OCR on exactly this kind of anti-aliased UI text, but classic VNRecognizeTextRequest via ocrmac is the well-trodden binding and is the one that returns per-line confidence and bounding boxes, which the app-first naming rule uses to make title-bar text outrank body text.

options.label: Classic VNRecognizeTextRequest at .accurate via ocrmac (default)
options.tradeoff: Stable, documented, gives bounding boxes that the app-first slug rule depends on; may extract measurably less text than Live Text on dark-mode or low-contrast captures.

options.label: Live Text path, falling back to classic
options.tradeoff: Potentially better text extraction, which is the input everything downstream depends on; a less-trodden binding, and bounding-box detail would need re-plumbing.

options.label: Benchmark both on 50 of your own screenshots and pick
options.tradeoff: Decides the question with your actual data instead of a blog post; costs a day of build time before the pipeline exists.
